title: Vega’s signs: deathbed desire for Christ, martyrs’ joy, Bernard on sudden conversion
source_text: XIX. Quae sint vero illa argumenta postea explicat ipsius Vegae verbis quae citat ex ejus lib. 9. super Concilium Trid. cap. 48. Illa, inquit Vega, pax & securitas quae plerosque migrare de hac vita, illud ardens desiderium quo charitas, quum fuerit perfecta, clamat, Cupio dissolvi & esse cum Christo; & laetitia, qua exultant, dum intelligentes sibi propinquum esse diem mortis, dicunt cum Davide, Laetatus sum in his quae dicta sunt mihi, in domum Domini ibimus. Heu mihi, quia incolatus meus prolongatus est. Alacritas etiam & admiranda constantia Martyrum, & despicientia tormentorum, quid aliud sunt nisi testimonia apertissima hujusmodi certitudinis, quam de sua justitia & gratia apud Deum habent? Non sic exultarent advenientem mortem, non sic illam desiderarent, non sic laetarentur in tormentis, neque tanta quiete & placiditate animi de hac vita discederent, qui haesitarent, & dubii seu ancipites essent de suo statu, vel quovismodo formidarent. Deinde postquam multa in hanc sententiam citavit ex Bernardo, ac praesertim haec verba ex Epistola ejus 107. Si superna eum miseratio respexerit, immiseritque spiritum compunctionis, ut ingemiscat, resipiscat, mutet vitam, domet carnem, amet proximum, clamet ad Deum, proponatque de caetero vivere Deo: ex hac superni luminis gratuita visitatione, & subita mutatione dexterae Excelsi, agnoscit se merito quidem, non jam irae, sed gratiae filium, quippe qui aeternum erga se divinae bonitatis experitur affectum. Tandem concludit, quod sicuti ii, qui ista in se sentiunt atque experiuutur, certi sunt secundum Bernardi sententiam, sine metu & formidine, de gratiae praesentia, ita certo noverunt se certos esse, neque in aliquo falli ita arbitrando. Nec tamen hic ulla contingit temeritas. Denique subjungit fidem quae est virtus infusa, mediate ad illam certitudinem inclinare, quia certitudo ista a sententiis Scripturae pendet, quamvis sit certitudine fidei multo inferior.
pass_a_gloss: But what those arguments are he afterward explains in Vega’s own words which he cites from his book 9 on the Council of Trent, chapter 48. That peace and security, says Vega, with which many migrate from this life; that ardent desire with which charity, when it has been perfected, cries, I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ; and the joy with which they exult when, understanding the day of death near, they say with David, I rejoiced in those things which were said to me, we will go into the house of the Lord. Woe is me, because my sojourning is prolonged. The alacrity also and admirable constancy of the martyrs, and their contempt of torments—what else are they but most open testimonies of this sort of certainty which they have concerning their righteousness and grace with God? They would not so exult at approaching death, so desire it, so rejoice in torments, nor depart this life with such quiet and placidity of mind, if they hesitated and were doubtful or double-minded about their state, or in any way feared. Then after citing many things to this effect from Bernard, and especially these words from his Epistle 107—If heavenly pity has looked upon him and sent the spirit of compunction, that he may groan, repent, change his life, tame the flesh, love his neighbor, cry to God, and propose henceforth to live to God: from this free visitation of heavenly light and sudden change of the right hand of the Most High he acknowledges himself indeed deservedly no longer a son of wrath but of grace, inasmuch as he experiences the eternal affection of divine goodness toward himself—he finally concludes that just as those who sense and experience these things in themselves are certain according to Bernard’s opinion, without dread and fear, of the presence of grace, so they certainly know that they are certain, and are not deceived in so judging. Nor yet does any rashness occur here. Finally he adds that faith which is an infused virtue mediately inclines to that certainty, because that certainty depends on the sentences of Scripture, although it is much inferior to the certainty of faith.
pass_b_english: Vega points to peaceful deaths, longing to be with Christ, and martyrs’ joy as signs of moral certainty of grace.
Bernard’s sudden conversion under heavenly light likewise yields fearless assurance short of strict faith-certainty.
